results.summary: Nicolas' first Wokwi design is a simple combinational circuit that displays a lowercase letter n when the correct inputs are driven high. The design is built from basic logic gates and is intended as a first introduction to the Wokwi and Tiny Tapeout workflow. It is tested by setting inputs IN0, IN1, IN3, IN5, and IN7 on with all others off. No external hardware beyond the simulator is required, and the project has essentially no documentation beyond the pin names.

This project implements a combinational logic circuit using NAND, NOT, AND, and OR gates to drive segments of a 7-segment display. The user applies binary inputs to the listed pins and observes the resulting gate outputs on the chip's outputs. It is intended as a basic digital logic exercise, likely from a workshop or class. The documentation is sparse and the provided test instructions are garbled, so the exact mapping from inputs to displayed digits is not clear. No external hardware is needed other than the simulator.

First Chip is a small combinational logic design that outputs signals to display the first letter of the author's name when a specific input pattern is applied. The design uses NOR, inverter, and AND gates to process six inputs. It is tested by setting the switches to the code 0000011, which activates the correct outputs. The documentation is very brief and does not specify which letter is displayed or how the outputs map to a display. No external hardware is used.

Rola_Tiny Tapeout Template Workshop4Mar26 is a workshop template design that lights up segments to form the letter A on a 7-segment display when all switches are turned on. The circuit is composed of multiple AND gates, each driving a segment. It is tested by setting all inputs to zero (display off) and then turning on switches connected to each AND gate to check individual segments. The project is clearly a teaching template for first-time Tiny Tapeout users and uses no external components beyond the simulator.

Akash's first Wokwi design implements a single NAND gate that takes two inputs and produces one output. The remaining pins are labeled as inputs or outputs but their function is not documented. The design appears to be a first experiment in digital logic and is tested by pressing the Wokwi button. No external hardware or detailed usage instructions are provided, and the one-line description is nonsensical, indicating very little documentation.

This project is a barely documented Wokwi design that appears to include a NAND gate and multiple input/output pins. The description fields are filled with placeholder text asking the user to explain how the project works and how to test it, so the actual function is unknown. There is no indication of external hardware or specific behavior. The design is likely an unfinished template or first attempt at a Tiny Tapeout submission.

This design displays the number 6 on a 7-segment display by default and switches to the number 7 when a button is held. Internally it uses a multiplexer to select between two input states and combinational logic to drive the segments. It is tested by holding down the "Step" button while observing the display change. No external hardware is required. The project is a basic digital logic exercise, likely from a computer science class.

This design tests a chain of AND and NOT gates by illuminating LEDs only when switches 6 and 7 are both turned on. It is a simple combinational logic experiment intended for educational purposes, with no other inputs affecting the outputs. The project is tested by flipping switches and observing the LEDs, and it requires a seven-segment LED device as external hardware. The documentation is minimal and does not explain the internal gate arrangement beyond the high-level description.

This project drives a 7-segment display based on input switches, using inputs d, e, and f to control lower segments while inputs a and b are routed through a multiplexer selected by input c. It functions as a basic test of pre-defined input-to-output mappings, likely for a workshop or class. Testing involves setting the switches and observing the displayed segments. External hardware includes a 7-segment display and switches, though in the simulator these are virtual. The documentation is brief and does not detail the exact segment mapping.

Joe's first Wokwi design converts a 5-bit binary input into a hexadecimal output suitable for driving a seven-segment display. The inputs are labeled e, d, c, b, a (with a as the least significant bit) and the outputs correspond to the eight display segments. It is tested by connecting switches to the inputs and a seven-segment display to the outputs, then cycling through binary values 0-9 to check the displayed digit. The design is intended as an educational exercise for a class or workshop and requires external hardware in a real setup.
